teaser.text: Caterpillar makes the machines and power systems that let people build, mine, transport goods and produce electricity. Its dollar comes in through equipment, parts, services and finance, then goes out through suppliers, employees, factories, lenders, taxes and the risks of keeping customers operating.

blocks.heading: Where could Caterpillar's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: At today’s $796.18, the weighted October 2027 price is $497.41, a 37% loss including dividends. In October 2028, the weighted price is $522.93, a 33% loss. In October 2029, it is $549.82, a 28% loss.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Caterpillar?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives operating profit of $11,400 million, then $12,012 million and $12,792 million. It applies margins below history because Construction dealer inventory is expected to fall by at least $1,000 million and Resource Industries already had $158 million of unfavorable manufacturing costs against $75 million of favorable pricing. The bull case reaches $15,470 million, $17,019 million and $19,190 million as engine capacity expands and backlog converts profitably.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Caterpillar really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow has other complications. Caterpillar’s 2022 reported figure included $717 million of tax-settlement payments that actually left the company. Stock compensation offers another analytical adjustment: subtracting it produced “real” free cash flow of $9,242 million in 2025. Capital spending also combines replacement and expansion, and Caterpillar does not disclose a clean maintenance figure.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Caterpillar today?

paragraphs.text: A share represents a claim on Caterpillar’s factories, power business, parts network and financing subsidiary. P/E means the dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit. A 34.3x trailing P/E implies about $23.21 of earnings per share from the past year, while the 24.6x forward P/E implies $32.37 from the next year. The lower forward multiple does not mean the stock became cheaper; it means expected profit is higher. At 20x earnings, today’s price would require about $39.81 per share.

dividend.meta_description: Caterpillar pays a rising dividend funded by cash, with growth tied to buybacks, power investment, dealer demand and today's yield.
dividend.opening: Caterpillar's dividend starts at a quarterly rate of $1.63, with the base path giving $6.64, $7.12 and $7.68 per share. Caterpillar's 2025 real free cash flow was $9,242 million, while Caterpillar distributed about $7.9 billion through dividends and repurchases, so cash covered those distributions.
dividend.closing: The full memo also answers how Caterpillar's business works, who its rivals are, how management allocates capital, and what risks could change the outlook.

blocks.heading: How much does Caterpillar pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends start from a quarterly rate of $1.63. The base path gives $6.64, $7.12 and $7.68 per share, while the bear holds at $6.52 and the bull reaches $8.08 by 2029. The base continues the company’s roughly 8% annual increases; the bear assumes a pause because expansion competes for cash. Caterpillar has raised its annual dividend for 32 consecutive years, supporting stability but not guaranteeing growth.

paragraphs.text: MP&E means Machinery, Power & Energy, excluding Financial Products. In 2025, MP&E operating cash flow was $12,278 million and capital spending was $2,794 million, leaving $9,484 million of free cash flow under the company’s definition. Cash generation held up even as earnings weakened, and Caterpillar distributed about $7.9 billion through dividends and repurchases.

Free cash flow has other complications. Caterpillar’s 2022 reported figure included $717 million of tax-settlement payments that actually left the company. Stock compensation offers another analytical adjustment: subtracting it produced “real” free cash flow of $9,242 million in 2025. Capital spending also combines replacement and expansion, and Caterpillar does not disclose a clean maintenance figure.

paragraphs.text: The bear view would gain weight in late 2026 and 2027 if dealer inventory falls faster than end-user demand, factory utilization weakens or supplier constraints delay profitable power deliveries. Slower cash generation would also limit repurchases.

blocks.heading: What is Caterpillar's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Industrial cash flow is the cleaner valuation test. The stated consolidated free-cash-flow yield is 2.6%, but group cash flow mixes factories with lending. Caterpillar expected 2026 industrial free cash flow in the top half of its $6 billion–$15 billion target range, or roughly $10.5 billion–$15 billion. Against today’s market value, that is about 2.9%–4.1%. The dividend yield is only 0.8%, so much of the investment case depends on future cash and repurchases.

earnings.title: Caterpillar earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: Caterpillar's next results are expected October 29, 2026; guidance covers sales, margin, cash flow, tariffs and restructuring costs.
earnings.opening: Caterpillar's next results are expected on October 29, 2026. Watch whether Caterpillar turns orders into profitable deliveries as dealers reduce inventory.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers how Caterpillar makes money, how it compares with rivals, who runs it, and what risks could disrupt it.

paragraphs.text: Second-quarter operating profit included **$392 million** of expected tariff recoveries. Management also said adjusted margin without expected recoveries would sit near the bottom of its target range, even though that range rises with sales. At **$72 billion** of annual sales, the stated range is **18–22%**.

Caterpillar’s industrial business, which it calls Machinery, Power & Energy, or MP&E, is expected to generate **$10,500–$15,000 million** of free cash flow in 2026. Free cash flow is operating cash after capital spending, so the planned **$3,500 million** of capital expenditure is already deducted. The plan also includes **$2,200 million** of tariff costs and **$300–$350 million** of restructuring costs.

blocks.heading: Has Caterpillar kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Services provide the other test. Caterpillar generated $24 billion of services revenue in 2025, below an earlier $28 billion aspiration. Its new target is $30 billion. Services include parts, repairs, maintenance, financing and digital support, turning the machines already operating in the field into continuing customer relationships. The global spare-parts market was estimated at $174.04 billion in 2025 and forecast at $264.12 billion in 2030; a major construction-equipment rival reported ¥145,226 million in parts and service revenue. The opportunity is large, but Caterpillar must show that added investment earns adequate returns.

blocks.heading: What is Caterpillar's recent revenue and profit trend?
What should Caterpillar watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: The next tests are whether Caterpillar converts orders into profitable deliveries and temporary benefits into dependable cash. Third-quarter results are scheduled for **October 29, 2026**, and should test the expected **$600 million** of third-quarter tariff costs.

That report should also show whether customer demand remains healthy as dealers reduce inventory. Shipments may slow because dealers are working through machines already on their lots, or because contractors and other end users need fewer machines. Those causes have very different meanings for Caterpillar’s future.
